blocks.how_it_works: A declaration of trust is the written instrument that creates a trust. The settlor states an intent to hold property for named beneficiaries and appoints a trustee to manage it. Under Wyoming law, the trust instrument must be signed by the settlor. Wyoming does not require witnesses for trust execution. Notarization is not required for the trust instrument itself, though it is recommended for practical purposes. The trust becomes active when it is funded: real property moves by a new deed to the trustee, and bank and brokerage accounts are retitled in the name of the trust or trustee. A successor trustee named in the document takes over if the acting trustee steps down, becomes incapacitated, or dies. When proof of the trust is needed, Wyo. Stat. § 4-10-1014 lists what a certification or affidavit of trust may contain, and a third party may require the trustee to furnish excerpts.

faq.q: Does Wyoming require notarization for a declaration of trust?
faq.a: Under Wyoming law, the trust instrument must be signed by the settlor. Wyoming does not require witnesses for trust execution. Notarization is not required for the trust instrument itself, though it is recommended for practical purposes. The certification of trust under Wyo. Stat. § 4-10-1014 may be signed or otherwise authenticated by any trustee; no notary or witness requirement is specified for the certification itself. Real property transferred to a trust must be recorded with the county clerk.

faq.q: Can Wyoming protect assets from the settlor's own creditors?
faq.a: Yes. Wyoming enacted a Domestic Asset Protection Trust (DAPT) statute under Wyo. Stat. § 4-10-505 (qualified spendthrift trusts), allowing self-settled asset protection trusts. The statute requires a qualified transfer affidavit sworn to by the settlor. The 4-year statute of limitations for fraudulent transfer claims (or 1 year from discovery) provides strong creditor protection. Wyoming also provides privacy protections in judicial proceedings involving trusts, with trust instruments and related documents receiving privacy protections upon filing of any petition.

faq.q: What goes in a certification of trust under Wyo. Stat. § 4-10-1014?
faq.a: The statute lists the contents: that the trust exists and the date the trust instrument was executed; the identity of the settlor; the identity and address of the currently acting trustee; the pertinent powers of the trustee; the revocability or irrevocability of the trust and the identity of any person holding a power to revoke; the authority of cotrustees to sign or otherwise authenticate and whether all or less than all are required to exercise powers of the trustee; the trust's taxpayer identification number (optional); and the manner of taking

faq.q: How does Wyoming treat business trusts?
faq.a: Wyoming recognizes statutory trusts under the Wyoming Statutory Trust Act (Wyo. Stat. § 17-29-101 et seq.), which provides for a flexible business entity similar to a Delaware statutory trust. A Wyoming statutory trust is a separate legal entity with limited liability for beneficial owners and trustees. Common law business trusts (Massachusetts trusts) are also recognized. The Wyoming Uniform Trust Code (Title 4, Chapter 10) applies to express trusts and does not directly govern statutory business trusts.

blocks.common_mistakes: Common issues include assuming Wyoming law requires witnesses or notarization for the trust instrument itself (it requires neither, though recording-related steps such as deeds require recording with the county clerk), and leaving the trust unfunded so that property never actually moves into it through a new deed or retitled accounts. Another frequent mix-up is treating Wyoming like a state without asset protection: Wyoming has a DAPT statute under § 4-10-505 that allows self-settled asset protection trusts with a qualified transfer affidavit. People also assume Wyoming's dynasty trust period is limited; the state has abolished the rule against perpetuities for qualifying trusts, allowing dynasty trusts to last up to 1,000 years. Documents that omit the statement that the trust has not been revoked or modified, or that do not match the certification requirements of § 4-10-1014, create avoidable friction during administration.
blocks.state_notes: Wyoming operates under Wyo. Stat. Title 4, Chapter 10 (Uniform Trust Code), including § 4-10-1014 (Certification or Affidavit of Trust), § 4-10-501 et seq. (Creditor's Claims; Spendthrift and Discretionary Trusts), and § 4-10-505 (Qualified Spendthrift Trusts / DAPT). The state levies no state income tax, no state estate tax, and no inheritance tax, making it one of the most trust-friendly states. Wyoming has abolished the Rule Against Perpetuities for qualifying trusts, allowing dynasty trusts to last up to 1,000 years. Wyoming enacted a DAPT statute under § 4-10-505, allowing self-settled asset protection trusts with a 4-year statute of limitations for fraudulent transfer claims. Wyoming also provides privacy protections in judicial proceedings involving trusts. The state supports flexible modification mechanisms including decanting, nonjudicial settlement agreements, and court-supervised modification. Wyoming adopted the UTC in 2003 but has heavily modified it to create a flexible, settlor-friendly framework.
